idiom_name: method decorator replacing the PropertyDescriptor (or NestJS NestInterceptor)
implementation_notes: TypeScript supplies an annotation-like seam: a method decorator receives the prototype and the PropertyDescriptor, so it can replace descriptor.value with an audited wrapper at class-definition time - the classic Interceptor plus InvocationContext structure becomes decorator metadata and the descriptor, and reflect-metadata is what makes the target's type information available. NestJS packages exactly this as a framework concept: a class implementing NestInterceptor with intercept(context, next) wraps the handler and is bound with @UseInterceptors. Where decorators cannot be applied (plain objects, dependencies), an ES Proxy or a wrapper function is the fallback, and the audit sink plus event schema still have to be written.
pitfalls: Decorators run once when the class is defined: a wrapper that captures a sink instance in a closure shares it across all instances - resolve per-call state (actor, sink) from this or a registry, not from the decorator's arguments.

Legacy decorators (experimentalDecorators) expect a PropertyDescriptor while TypeScript 5 standard decorators receive (value, context); copying a decorator between the two modes silently produces a wrapper that never runs.
Async methods must not be wrapped with a synchronous try/catch: return the promise and record the outcome in then/catch, otherwise a rejected call is recorded as a success before it settles.
